title: Nana Asma'u's verses
hook: the Sokoto scholar's poems for teaching women
tomorrow: why would a book keep the views its author thinks are wrong?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Iqbal's Complaint: a complaint, and an answer, both spoken to God. Today the last of the poets, who wrote poems to be carried home.
screen: `A COMPLAINT, AND AN ANSWER.` → `TODAY, POEMS THAT TRAVEL.`

segments.voice: The alphabet song. A jingle from an old ad you can't shake. Rhythm holds on to things long after a page is lost. Now, a road out of Sokoto, in what is now northern Nigeria. A woman is walking home to her village, and she's carrying something she can't drop: a poem, memorized line by line from the scholar who wrote it, Nana Asma'u. When she gets home, the women of her village will gather around her, and she'll teach it to them, line by line, until they know it too. That's how you teach a whole village with a poem.
screen: `RHYTHM HOLDS ON.` → `A ROAD OUT OF SOKOTO.` → `A POEM SHE CAN'T DROP.`

segments.voice: Nana Asma'u was a scholar and poet, the daughter of Usman dan Fodio, the teacher who founded the Sokoto state. She wrote in the languages the people around her spoke, not only in Arabic, and she wrote to teach. Not every woman she wanted to reach could read. So she put the lessons in verse: the life of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, how to live and pray, how to grieve. In one poem she names holy women of Islam, from the Prophet's household onward, so women listening heard their own place in the story. Then came the clever part. Women came to her as students, learned the poems, and walked back to teach women in their villages. They were called the 'Yan Taru, those who come together. A poem doesn't need a school building, a printing press, or anyone's permission. It needs one person who knows it by heart and a circle willing to listen. Teaching in verse turned every student into a teacher, and every kitchen into a classroom.
screen: `A SCHOLAR, DAUGHTER OF A TEACHER.` · `LESSONS PUT INTO VERSE.` · `HOLY WOMEN, NAMED IN A POEM.` · `THE 'YAN TARU CARRY IT HOME.` · then, large: `TEACHING IN VERSE.`

segments.voice: Choose a line you already know by heart and would want to pass on: a verse, a saying from someone you love, a line from this path. Say it aloud slowly, tapping the beat on your knee. Then once more, softer, as if teaching it to someone younger.
screen: `A LINE YOU'D PASS ON.` · `SAY IT, TAP THE BEAT.` · `ONCE MORE, AS A TEACHER.`

howItsDone: In northern Nigeria, women's study circles still teach and sing Nana Asma'u's poems; Muslim teachers elsewhere also use rhymed verse to help children learn prayer, the Prophet's life and the basics of faith.
